summary: In Greek mythology, Hermione was the daughter of Menelaus, king of Sparta, and Helen of Troy. Betrothed first to her cousin Orestes, she was later promised to Achilles' son Neoptolemus as a prize of the Trojan War. After Neoptolemus' death at Delphi she married Orestes and bore Tisamenus, continuing the Spartan-Mycenaean royal line.
etymology: Ancient Greek Hermiónē; the personal name is separate from the Argolic city Hermione.

sections.heading: Betrothals
paragraphs: Before the Trojan War, Tyndareus betrothed Hermione to Orestes. Apollodorus says she was nine when Helen left with Paris. During the war Menelaus promised her instead to Neoptolemus; Euripides' Andromache has Orestes call Menelaus a liar for that switch, while Ovid's Heroides has Hermione insist Tyndareus acted without Menelaus' knowledge.
Homer's Odyssey places her wedding to Neoptolemus ten years after Troy: when Telemachus visits Sparta, Menelaus is holding the marriage feast as he sends his daughter to Achilles' son.

sections.heading: Neoptolemus and Andromache
paragraphs: At Phthia Hermione quarreled with Andromache, Hector's widow and Neoptolemus' war-prize concubine. In Euripides she blames Andromache's spells for her own childlessness and seeks to have her killed while Neoptolemus is away at Delphi; Peleus intervenes.
Neoptolemus dies at Delphi — slain by a priest, temple servants, Apollo, or by Orestes, according to variant accounts. Orestes then takes Hermione to Mycenae to fulfill the original betrothal.

sections.heading: Marriage to Orestes
paragraphs: Hermione and Orestes marry; their son Tisamenus becomes heir of the Atreid line in the Peloponnese. Some notices also give Orestes a marriage to Erigone, without clarifying Hermione's fate. Later lore places Hermione with her parents in Elysium; a scholion on Pindar, citing Ibycus, even has her marry the apotheosized Diomedes among the Dioscuri.
Her story fed later art and drama, from Racine's Andromaque to Rossini's Ermione.
